original.1.2:
Welcome back to the AI Confidence Academy. In the previous lesson, you practiced taking responsibility for the work AI helps you produce. You checked the facts before accepting a polished report. Today, we go one step earlier. Before we ask AI to build something, we ask whether we understand the actual need.

Imagine someone says, “We need a chatbot.” A chatbot might help. But why do they need it? Are customers missing information? Are employees using different instructions? Are questions reaching the wrong person? Those are different problems, and they may need different solutions.

Today, you'll learn to separate a visible symptom from its possible cause. You'll compare three needs, investigate the evidence, and use your own AI assistant to prepare fair questions rather than invent answers. By the end, you'll select one provisional need for the project you began in Lesson 1.1. Your decision will be open to correction when better evidence arrives.

You bring the purpose and judgment. AI can help you organize what you know and ask what you still need to learn. Let's begin with the person who needs the work to improve.
original.1.3:
Welcome back to the AI Confidence Academy. In the last lesson, you started with people and their needs. You compared possible problems, distinguished observations from assumptions, and chose one need to investigate. Today we will decide which parts of that work deserve help from AI—and which parts do not.

A business owner can save twenty minutes using AI to draft a proposal, then spend thirty minutes correcting promises the business never made. The draft was faster. The full job was not. That distinction matters whenever someone says AI saves time.

You'll match five tasks with appropriate support, compare an AI approach with a simpler non-AI alternative, and choose a measure of useful value. You will use the AI assistant you already chose, but your judgment—and your evidence—will determine the final decision.

We are not collecting AI tricks. We are developing professional ability to choose when a tool serves a real purpose. Let's begin.
original.1.4:
Welcome back to the AI Confidence Academy. You have identified a need worth investigating, examined where AI may help, and learned to measure business value rather than simply counting outputs. Today we will bring those decisions into a professional conversation with AI.

An AI assistant can produce an attractive recommendation in seconds. But if you have not supplied the purpose, the person it serves, the necessary facts, and the limitations, that recommendation may only sound convincing.

In this lesson you will learn a Professional Request Framework built around six essentials: purpose, audience, context, task, constraints and quality. Then you will ask your own AI assistant to compare two options, challenge an unsupported assumption, and decide what evidence you still need.

Your final responsibility is not to accept the recommendation. It is to make a decision you can explain and defend. We will practice with a fictional founder who has a promising business idea, but not yet enough facts to choose a service. Let's begin.
original.1.5:
Welcome back to the AI Confidence Academy. We are now in Phase Two, Journey One, Lesson Five: Scope a Solution and a Project Worth Completing.

You have investigated a real need, selected appropriate AI roles, examined potential value, and practiced making professional requests supported by evidence. Today, we will turn that thinking into the beginning of something you can actually finish.

An ambitious project can sound impressive while remaining too large to complete. A modest, well-defined project can demonstrate far more. We will use the FOCUS Capstone Frame to clarify the function, owner, customer, use case and scope of your work. Then you will compare three possible artifacts, identify necessary permissions, and decide exactly what your first useful result will include—and what it will leave out.

Your AI assistant can help you examine options and simplify a plan. It cannot authorize a client commitment, invent access to information, or decide what another person has approved.

By the end, you will have a compact project charter and solution concept that you can carry into the rest of Phase Two.

Let's begin.
original.1.6:
Welcome back to the AI Confidence Academy. We are now in Phase Two, Journey One, Lesson Six: Stress Test the Professional Operating Model.

You have reached the final lesson of our first journey. Across these lessons, you have identified a need, examined where AI support makes sense, measured potential business value, practiced directing professional requests, and scoped a capstone project you can actually finish.

Today, we will put those decisions under pressure. A useful professional operating model must guide you when things go smoothly—and when an AI answer is wrong, a source is outdated, or a request carries consequences for other people.

You will combine your responsibilities, review steps, boundaries and development commitments into one operating model. Then you will test it against three situations: a routine task, an inaccurate answer and a high-consequence request involving privacy or authority. You will identify a rule that needs strengthening, revise it, and defend a decision to proceed as well as a decision to pause.

This completes Journey One's foundation. The model you produce will continue with your project throughout Phase Two. It does not replace human judgment. It makes your judgment clear and accountable.

Let's begin.
original.2.1:
Welcome back to the AI Confidence Academy. We are now in Phase Two, Journey Two, Lesson One: Map the Work and Locate Friction.

In Journey One, you defined a real need, clarified where AI could help, and created a professional operating model and a finishable project charter. Today, we'll use that same project to examine how the work actually moves from beginning to end.

A process may look simple until a request reaches the next person and stops. In our fictional example, an estimate waits three days because nobody owns the missing specifications. Automating the final email won't solve that problem.

You'll map the people, inputs, steps, decisions, tools, handoffs, and review. Then you'll locate three points of friction and check whether they reflect real causes or only assumptions. Your own AI assistant can help organize the map, but you will verify it and choose one responsible improvement.

We're moving from project direction into practical business workflows. We'll build on the evidence you already have, without starting over.

Let's begin.
original.2.2:
Welcome back to the AI Confidence Academy. We are in Phase Two, Journey Two, Lesson Two: Produce Communication That Serves the Audience.

In our last lesson, you mapped how work moves through people, information, decisions, and review. Today, we will use that map to identify a message that helps someone take the next step.

A polished message can still leave its reader confused. A customer may need two missing details explained and a realistic response time. A manager may need a clear account of what is waiting and who owns the next action. Both need accurate facts, expressed for their situation.

You will use the Professional Request Framework to direct your own AI assistant. You will give it approved facts and a sample of your intended voice, improve one draft, and adapt it for another audience or channel without changing its meaning.

You will also check for missing information, unsupported promises, and summaries that leave out an important condition. Keep the original and revised communication in your continuing Project Record. In the next lesson, we will apply the full CLEAR quality review.

Let's begin.
original.2.3:
Welcome back to the AI Confidence Academy. We are in Phase Two, Journey Two, Lesson Three: Verify and Revise with CLEAR.

In the previous lesson, you produced a communication for a specific audience and adapted it without changing the facts. Today, we will examine that draft before anyone relies on it.

A proposal may promise delivery in five days even though no one has confirmed the capacity to do the work. Making the sentence sound more confident does not make the promise true.

You will use the Academy's CLEAR quality review: Correct, Listener, Enough, Appropriate, and Responsible. First, you will review the draft yourself. Then you will ask your own AI assistant for additional critique and compare its suggestions with your judgment.

You will verify at least one important claim against an authoritative source or approved record, revise the communication, and identify the person who can approve it. AI checking its own answer does not provide independent evidence.

Keep the original draft, your source and date, the changes you made, and any remaining limits in your continuing Project Record. The purpose is work you can explain and support, with people responsible for its use.

Let's begin.
original.2.4:
Welcome back to the AI Confidence Academy. This is Phase Two, Journey Two, Lesson Four: Choose Assistants, Automation and Agents.

In Lesson Three, you reviewed your communication with CLEAR, checked an important claim, and kept human approval visible. Now we will decide how much support your workflow actually needs.

An assistant can help prepare a reply. A rule-based automation can follow a fixed instruction. An agent may plan and take several steps within its permissions. And sometimes a clear checklist and a person are enough.

We will compare all four choices using one practical case: an invoice reminder. A routine reminder is different from a disputed charge. Drafting a message is different from sending it, changing a balance, or approving a refund.

You will choose the least complex suitable approach for your continuing project. You will name what it may do, what it must never do, who reviews the result, and when the work must stop and return to a person.

Then you will check any platform claim against current official documentation and save your comparison and updated solution concept. Today we are planning a bounded approach. We are not connecting accounts or deploying a live system.

Let's begin.
original.2.5:
Welcome back to the AI Confidence Academy. This is Phase Two, Journey Two, Lesson Five: Build a Bounded Working Prototype.

In Lesson Four, you chose a suitable support pattern and defined its permissions, human checkpoints, and fallback. Now we will turn that concept into a working sample.

A prototype helps you learn whether an idea is useful. It can be a prompt-supported document process, an approved template, or an authorized sandbox workflow. Start with one narrow path that you can run from input to a reviewed result.

We will use the BUILD Evidence Cycle: baseline, use AI, inspect, lead, and demonstrate. In our fictional proposal case, the prototype drafts an outline from supplied specifications and highlights missing information. A person still checks scope and prices before any real proposal is issued.

For your continuing project, you will define the input, acceptance criteria, review owner, and completion signal. Then you will run a realistic normal case, preserve the actual output, and make one material revision.

You will save the working artifact, baseline, test evidence, and before-and-after results. You will demonstrate what the sample does, explain its limits, and keep approval with the authorized person. A description alone is not a completed prototype.

Let's begin.
original.2.6:
Welcome back to the AI Confidence Academy. This is Phase Two, Journey Two, Lesson Six: Test Errors and Exception Paths.

In Lesson Five, you built a bounded working prototype, ran a normal case, and made a material revision. Now we will find out what happens when the work becomes incomplete, contradictory, or outside the agreed scope.

A useful sample must do more than produce a good-looking result. It must make uncertainty visible, avoid unauthorized action, and give the person a clear way to review and correct the work.

Our fictional proposal case receives two different participant counts. The right response is to flag the conflict and ask for clarification. Choosing one number silently creates an unsupported result.

You will define expected behavior before each test, then preserve the actual input, request, output, and finding. You will test the normal path, missing information, conflicting specifications, and a request outside scope.

Then you will correct one observed failure and retest the same case. You will compare the evidence, update your workflow map and solution concept, and explain the human control point that remains.

To complete Journey Two, you will assemble your communication evidence, maps, concept, and working artifact in the continuing Project Record. Keep unresolved defects visible and carry the saved work into Journey Three.

Let's begin.

Welcome back to the AI Confidence Academy. We are beginning Phase Two, Journey One, Lesson One: Professional AI Judgment and Direction.

You have learned to work with generative AI. Now we begin a different kind of practice: using those skills to produce work that is useful, can be checked, and has someone clearly responsible for the outcome.

In this lesson, we start with a familiar professional situation. A manager needs a weekly service report. AI helps organize the information into a clear summary. The writing looks finished, but one of its figures cannot be traced to the source notes.

What happens next is the heart of today's lesson.

Rather than accepting a polished answer, we will examine the source record, inspect the draft, identify the claim that needs evidence, and revise the report. You will see those steps on screen. Then you'll decide for yourself what should be kept, corrected, or withheld.

After that, we turn to a task from your work, a business you are developing, or a professional opportunity you want to explore. You will identify five capabilities you can already demonstrate, along with the evidence that supports them, and two areas where you still need to develop. Be specific. We are not making a list of tools you have tried. We are identifying abilities you can put to work and explain to another person.

Next, you will build your first human-and-AI responsibility map. You'll describe the purpose of the task, which parts an AI system may assist with, what information must be checked, and who makes the final decision. You'll use an AI assistant of your choosing to examine your notes and identify what may be missing.

The important work begins when you examine the result. Did the system add an ability you never claimed? Did it assume authority you do not have? Did it include a figure that needs an independent source? You will make a correction, explain why it matters, and keep the evidence in your Project Record.

That first record becomes part of the business project you will develop throughout Phase Two. The goal today is not to build a complicated automation. It is to establish the professional judgment that will make the workflows and systems you build worth trusting.

You'll watch the example, practice the method, and finish with a result you can explain.

At the Academy, we put it simply: AI assists. Humans verify.

Let's begin.
